AI is reading scans, interpreting pathology, predicting clinical deterioration and transcribing consultations. My one concern is whether our regulators have the powers, resources and capacity to enforce the protections effectively. Introducing legislation is only half the battle. The Government must ensure that the businesses that breach such consumer laws are held accountable, and that bodies such as trading standards and the Competition and Markets Authority have the tools they need to take meaningful action. Consumers deserve not only protections on paper, but the confidence that those protections will be enforced in practice. Ultimately, people should not need to navigate pages of jargon or jump through hoops just to get a fair deal. They deserve transparency and the choice and freedom to walk away. This legislation is an important step towards that. I hope it will be backed by that continued action; I hope the Minister will be able to continue the progress that she is already making and will have further announcements, particularly on additional support for trading standards, for example, which we know has been quite reduced. hansard.speaker: Dame Meg Hillier (Hackney South and Shoreditch) (Lab/Co-op)

hansard.speaker: Callum Anderson (Buckingham and Bletchley) (Lab)

hansard.speaker: Baroness Harding of Winscombe (Con)

However, we really want to have much more stable and permanent regulatory guardrails for this future technology, so implementing these recommendations is really important. It is tempting to think it is just about going down a list of actions and ticking them off, but this is really complex work because AI products are not the same as other medical devices. AI in healthcare is going to evolve once it is out of the lab and in the healthcare system. The MHRA, therefore, cannot just approve something or not approve it; we are going to need a different approach to regulating. As the commission itself said, it needs to be both “more proportionate” and “lifecycle-based”, it has to follow the AI out into the real world and it needs to involve the whole system, not just the “manufacturer”. hansard.speaker: Lord Tarassenko (CB)
hansard.text: My Lords, I will speak to Amendment 172D in my name, to which the noble Baroness, Lady Harding of Winscombe, and the noble Lord, Lord Clement-Jones, have added their names. I declare my interests as senior adviser to the Alan Turing Institute, director of LIO Health, and the holder of an honorary contract with Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust. When an AI algorithm has a medical purpose, such as diagnosing, monitoring or guiding treatment, it is regulated as a medical device under the UK Medical Devices Regulations 2002, and the regulator is the MHRA. So how quickly AI can be safely adopted in the NHS depends largely on MHRA and regulations written more than 20 years ago.

hansard.speaker: Baroness Shawcross-Wolfson (Con)
hansard.text: My Lords, I will speak briefly in support of Amendment 203 in the name of the noble Baroness, Lady Ritchie of Downpatrick. As other noble Lords have said, there are two key principles at play here. The first is the need to modernise the law to reflect changes in technology, an issue we have discussed in an earlier group of amendments and that my noble friend Lady Harding set out very clearly. Injectables used to mean conventional syringes and needles; now they frequently come in the form of a pen that can be safely used by patients themselves. As technology has changed, the products and the risks have changed. Regulations should change too, from blanket prohibition to case-by-case consideration. The second principle here is the need to remove unnecessary barriers to healthcare for patients, both to improve their experience and to create a more efficient NHS. As the noble Baroness, Lady Gerada, set out, this is incredibly important across the NHS. When I was in government, I had the privilege to work on the introduction of Pharmacy First, and I am delighted that the Government have continued to support this programme. The policy is simple: where a patient can safely get treatment from a pharmacist, we should make that possible. The same principle applies here: where a treatment can safely be given over the counter, we should make that possible. hansard.speaker: Lord McColl of Dulwich (Con)
hansard.text: My Lords, I will speak to Amendment 141, to which my noble friend Lord Prior has given his support. It is a simple one, about the single patient record and who can be on it. It merely states that providers of care, including digital and non-NHS, can participate in the single patient record. This is firstly a matter of patient safety and continuity of care. An increasing number of people in the NHS are accessing medications and treatments outside the traditional pathways: online, through pharmacies, and independent of the NHS. A report by the HSSIB earlier this year drew attention to the practice of online prescriptions, which it found to be lacking: the information was rather confusing and it was being shared with the NHS and independent prescribers. That creates a risk. The finding is simple but profound. Having incomplete histories of patients inevitably leads to poor healthcare on either side of the public sector. A single patient record must contain every single medication and treatment, including those that derive from digital providers. Otherwise, the principle of the clause is completely undermined, as is patient safety and the doctor's ability to choose the best course of action. This in no way means unrestricted access. Secondary legislation will work out the appropriate safeguards. This will be limited to genuine care purposes, with suitable data protection requirements. The principle is clear: good-quality care and medication should not be excluded because they lie beyond the traditional means. Pharmacies in particular will benefit from having access to the record. In my professional life, I have seen nothing but excellence and diligence from pharmacies, be they in hospital or outside, and their ability to provide immediate, high-quality care to patients. Thi

hansard.speaker: Baroness Merron (Lab)
hansard.text: I can probably be more helpful on the second point than on the first at this stage. I cannot directly answer the questions raised by noble Lords about publication, but I can undertake to keep noble Lords updated on where we are with the review and the expectations that will follow its completion by Mr Lock. On Amendments 272 and 279R, we recognise that fertility treatment, as has been spoken of in this debate, has changed significantly since the Act was first introduced in 1990. That was highlighted by a number of noble Lords, including the noble Baronesses, Lady Deech, Lady Owen, Lady Pidgeon and Lady Shawcross-Wolfson. The HFEA has emphasised that the regulatory framework should reflect changes in how patients access information and treatment decisions, including with regard to the growth of online platforms, which could not have been considered way back in 1990, as we know. The amendments would make extensive and complex changes to the existing framework. It is our view—I know noble Lords will understand this—that changes of this scale require careful consideration of their legal and operational implications, alongside appropriate consultation and scrutiny. As I have said to noble Lords in many ways—so please forgive me for trying what is not really a different way—I can confirm that the Government are considering legislative options for reform in what is a very complex area and for when parliamentary time allows. I am sure we all agree that any future reform has to support patient safety and reflect societal change. The noble Baroness, Lady Gerada, made a good point about how the regulatory regime needs to reflect technological change as well as the market.

hansard.speaker: Irene Campbell
hansard.text: I thank the hon. Member for that point and I look forward to hearing the Minister's response to it. Under the previous system, bereavement payment and widowed parent's allowance were uprated annually with inflation, as was laid out in the Social Security Administration Act 1992. Most benefits are uprated every year to stay in line with inflation, but some, such as bereavement support payment and some extra cost disability benefits, are at the discretion of the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions. If the rates for bereavement support payment had been increased in line with the consumer price index, the lump sum payments are estimated to be £4,822 for those with dependent children and £3,445 for those on the standard rate. The petition was started by Caroline Booth, who is in the Public Gallery. Caroline took the time to meet me and tell her story. Caroline was married to her husband, Steve, for 25 years. She left her job to care for him and returned to work only two days after he died. She was widowed with two sons to care for, and she found out about bereavement support payment from the funeral director, but there is nothing mandatory in place to ensure that bereaved people get that information. Surely, that must be a matter for consideration. Since then, Caroline set up the campaign team called Widow's Fight. With that team, she has worked tirelessly on her campaign, gaining more than 100,000 signatures to this petition and the support of UK charities and many MPs, as well as growing a large social media following.

hansard.debate: State Pension:  Impact of Ending the Triple Lock
hansard.speaker: Baroness Sherlock (Lab)
hansard.text: The noble Baroness made a number of points. To be clear, the same percentage increase will apply both to those on the basic state pension and to those on the new state pension. That is the same percentage increase applied to the main rates of the state pension as now. Of course, the triple lock does not apply to additional elements. The basic state pension pensions are different: they had an earlier retirement age, and many of them contracted out and have additional pensions. Their circumstances are different. However, the noble Baroness is absolutely right that pension credit is the key to this. When the Labour Government introduced pension credit in the early 2000s, pensioner poverty after housing costs was around 25%. It has now come down to 14% and is projected to come down still further. It is not currently possible to do what the noble Baroness described with data matching because we do not hold enough data. We have just run the biggest-ever campaign to take up pension credit, with all kinds of advertising on social media, television and radio, and a big link-up with ITV's “The Chase”, which I am sure most noble Lords have noticed.

hansard.speaker: Lord Scriven (LD)
hansard.text: My Lords, Amendment 222 in my name asks one question: is a young boy in England protected by the same basic safeguards as we expect of any other surgical procedure performed on a child? At present, for non-therapeutic male circumcision, he is not. I am grateful to the noble Lord, Lord Birt, for adding his name to this amendment. Let me be clear about what this amendment does not do. It does not ban non-therapeutic male circumcision. It asks that, when a blade is taken to a child, the person holding it is qualified, the setting is safe and someone is accountable when things go wrong. That is a safeguarding principle, and safeguarding does not stop at the door of any one community. Under the law as it stands, anyone can legally circumcise a boy in this country with no medical training and no proven expertise. There is no minimum age to become a circumciser and no requirement to use an anaesthetic. A doctor struck off for dangerous circumcision can carry on circumcising boys as a lay person. Losing their licence removes the oversight, not the practice. The consequences are not theoretical. At least five boys have died after circumcision in recent years from haemorrhaging or sepsis, and in the four most recent cases, the person who performed the procedure had no qualifications to perform surgery. More boys in this country are now dying from circumcision than girls from female genital mutilation, a practice this House rightly treats as a matter of child protection. In February 2023, six month-old Mohamed Abdisamad was circumcised in west London by a circumciser recommended to his parents. A week later, he suffered cardiorespiratory arrest in an ambulance on the way to the hospital and died from an infection following the procedure. The coroner found no requirement for traini

hansard.speaker: Lord Clement-Jones (LD)
hansard.text: On the assumption that the Whips are not getting up at this time, since we are not quite there, I will speak to my Amendments 132, 145 and 146, which deal with the question of how the SPR protects sensitive and confidential clinical information, how patients can audit and challenge unauthorised access, and how Parliament scrutinises the regulations that will govern it. The events reported in the Guardian on Friday and the investigation since opened by the Information Commissioner's Office should be an urgent wake-up call to the Government as regards the SPR. A patient receiving psychotherapy at South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust discovered, by chance, while looking at her GP's screen, that detailed, deeply personal notes from her therapy sessions had been uploaded to the London Care Record, a system accessible to more than 100,000 NHS staff across London, including staff outside the trust treating her. When she discovered this, she felt forced to withdraw from mental health treatment during a family bereavement. In her letter of 22 November, the Minister stated that “there is no intention to simply make available widely the most sensitive information”, and notes that clinicians will be able to restrict access just as they do now. Yet the London Care Record case exposes the flaw in relying on administrative guidance and ministerial intention rather than binding statutory safeguards. First, when the South London and Maudsley and the London Care Record were challenged, neither was able to confirm whether all accesses were legitimate. We understand that the ICO has had to establish who is even acting as data controller, while downstream environments such as OneLondon have drawn data collected for direct care into secondary-use platforms. hansard.speaker: Kate Dearden
hansard.text: I thank hon. Members for their interventions and remarks on this legislation today. I am pleased to have the support of Opposition Members on this important legislation. Colleagues have outlined why it is necessary. My hon. Friend the Member for Tamworth mentioned transparency, choice and freedom, which are key. Colleagues mentioned the commencement period starting from January. As I mentioned in my speech, we want consumers to benefit from the protections as soon as possible. Consumers navigate difficult and complex processes with businesses if they want to cancel a subscription, which is why we are legislating here today. Providing that transparency is key, particularly when we look to January as a time when people might consider budgets and might want to take out or cancel subscriptions to a gym membership— [ Interruption. ] I did not look at anyone there—so we want to ensure that these rights are in place. It is a key time for consumers to be able to keep hold and have control of their hard-earned cash. We heard reflections on a grace period. hansard.speaker: Sarah Edwards (Tamworth) (Lab)
hansard.text: It is an honour to serve under your chairship, Mrs Jardine. This legislation about subscription contracts is not simply a step towards greater fairness and transparency for consumers; it is another example of how this Government are standing up for ordinary working people. It is about rebalancing the playing field and tackling businesses that have used complicated terms and conditions to lock people into unwanted subscriptions or roll them on to expensive contracts without their knowledge. That has obviously applied to many people, whether for gym memberships, food delivery services or digital streaming products: almost everything can now be bought on a subscription. The exploitation has been hidden behind unnecessary complexity. People spend their hard-earned money on things that make their lives a little better, only to be caught in subscriptions that they no longer want and to struggle to cancel them before they pay for more than they ever intended. Although the companies may not technically be deceiving their customers, they are repeatedly misleading them, through a smoke-and-mirrors approach that makes it far too easy to sign up and far too difficult—or even impossible—to leave. Consumers should be able to trust that when they sign up for something, they will receive what they were promised at the price they were promised and will have a straightforward way of cancelling when a service no longer suits them. That is the basic expectation, yet consumers are let down time and again. Such subscription traps are estimated to cost consumers around £170 per person each year, a significant sum. hansard.speaker: Bradley Thomas (Bromsgrove) (Con)
hansard.text: It is a pleasure to serve under your chairmanship, Ms Jardine. As the cost of living continues to rise, every pound matters more than ever for households across the country, and unwanted subscriptions can be far more than an inconvenience. An unexpected charge from a forgotten trial or automatic renewal can wipe out money budgeted for essentials, putting serious strain on a household's finances. Approximately 5.8% of active subscriptions, totalling 9.7 million and costing £2.1 billion annually in 2026 prices, are unwanted. Of those, an estimated 3.6 million are rolled over from free or discounted trials, while roughly 1.3 million came from auto-renewals. We want consumers to have protection from subscription providers that use misleading tactics and hidden renewals, while allowing for a fair and trustworthy relationship with legitimate providers. On the matter of legitimate providers, I am aware that leading fresh food delivery companies have expressed concerns about the proposed 14-day cooling-off rules failing to account for how perishable goods are sourced, prepared and delivered. hansard.speaker: Kate Dearden
hansard.text: It is a pleasure to serve under your chairship this evening, Mrs Jardine. These regulations, which were laid in draft before this House on 19 October, implement the subscriptions chapter in the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, known as the DMCCA. For consumers who enter subscription contracts, they offer new protections against being stuck in unwanted contracts. We estimate that there are around 155 million active subscriptions in the United Kingdom. However, although they bring convenience for both businesses and consumers, if they trick or trap consumers into subscriptions they do not want, they can be a source of consumer harm. Subscriptions should be a choice, not a trap, but I frequently receive letters from members of the public saying that they assumed a purchase was a one-off, but then discovered that money continued to leave their account each month. Often these are individuals on low incomes, so even small, unexpected costs create financial worry and hardship. I suspect I am not alone on this Committee in receiving those letters. I am also sure that many in this House have had the experience of signing up to a free trial, only to end up stuck in a costly subscription, because it auto-renewed without warning; or perhaps they have tried to end a subscription, but given up, because the business only allows cancellation by phone and they simply did not have the time. These new rules will put an end to these practices, which frustrate consumers, waste their time and, ultimately, cost them money. We estimate that consumers spend £2.1 billion each year on subscriptions they do not actually want. The subscription regulations implement four broad measures to tackle these problems. First, consumers must have clear information when they sign up. Secon

hansard.speaker: Lord Scriven (LD)
hansard.text: I know that the Minister was rushing through, but there were a lot of confused faces over who is the controller for the single patient record. We heard that individual GP practices were, for their data, but did the Minister say that the Secretary of State was the data controller for the single patient record, or is that still to be determined?

hansard.speaker: Lord Bradley (Lab)
hansard.text: My Lords, I will very briefly ask a question associated with this group of amendments. At Second Reading, I asked my noble friend the Minister to clarify the Government's position on access to the single patient record regarding the criminal justice system and its interface with healthcare. I have not yet received a reply, so I will ask again tonight. In the Minister's letter dated 7 October, she states that relevant healthcare professionals providing direct care in criminal justice settings will be able to access the single patient record information, but that this would not give police, courts and other criminal justice personnel general access to the single patient record. However, in responding to the debate on Amendment 90 from the noble Lord, Lord Foster of Bath, last week, the Minister said: “ICBs will have responsibilities for most of the health commissioning pathway from prisons and, to pick up the point about movement, to and from the community … There will be national rules in place to identify which ICB has responsibility for care, and the single patient record will be greatly helpful in ensuring that health information follows the person ”.—[ Official Report , 17/11/26; col. 690.] Will the Minister today provide a clear definition of direct care and confirm that, for example, liaison and diversion staff, especially mental health nurses, who are providing crucial direct care in police stations, courts, prisons, street triage and the community, will have access to these essential records?

hansard.speaker: Baroness Freeman of Steventon (CB)
hansard.text: My Lords, at the request of the noble Baroness, Lady Noakes, who is unable to be here today, and with the leave of the Committee, I am the last noble Baroness standing to move Amendment 130, to which I have added my name. I will also briefly speak in support of Amendments 135, 145 and 146 in this group, to which I have also added my name. These amendments are all to do with our rights as patients to control who sees our health data and for what purposes, and to check that it is being used for the purposes we have specified. I start with Amendment 130, which would simply allow patients to opt out of all or any information about them being shared in the single patient record. The single patient record is proposed in order to improve our individual healthcare and there are potentially big advantages to it. However, if individuals want to take the informed decision to opt out of that system, I do not see why they should not have the right to do so. Having our data in the single patient record has potential benefits and possible risks for us as individuals, and different people can legitimately come to different conclusions about the balance of those risks and benefits. As a patient, I have the right to opt out of life-saving care, such as a blood transfusion or chemotherapy, if I am judged competent to make that decision. Given that I can make that decision, what possible reason could there be for not allowing me to make the decision that I do not want my medical data to be shared as part of the single patient record? I cannot see a credible technical reason for denying an opt-out, and no research or planning reason could ethically override my rights as an individual to be able to determine the usage of my own health data. Amendment 135 in the name of the noble Lord, Lord K

hansard.speaker: Baroness Finlay of Llandaff (CB)
hansard.text: I would be most grateful if the Minister clarified further the overall governance and the Caldicott guardianship over the data. Will GPs be responsible for verifying that all the data inserted in the single patient record is accurate, or will they have indemnity only for information they insert? What will happen if they take a clinical decision on information that has been wrongly inserted from somewhere else, or the wrong terminology has been used, or there has been a spelling mistake, which could easily happen, which leads to, in effect, a malpractice action?

hansard.speaker: Baroness Thornton (Lab)
hansard.text: My Lords, Amendment 134 is in my name and that of my noble friend Lord Hunt. I declare two interests. I am a non-executive member of the Whittington Hospital, where we are embarking right now on the procurement process for our single patient record. I am also the chair of the Social Care Institute for Excellence. It is social care that I want to talk about. I thank my noble friend for the wonderfully helpful letter that we all received. Well, I thought it was helpful.

hansard.speaker: Baroness Merron (Lab)
hansard.text: My Lords, I am grateful for what I know is widespread overall support for the single patient record, and I appreciate the points that noble Lords have raised. I will do my best to address the broad sweep, but in view of the time, and because we wish to get to the next group—at least to start it—which is linked, I hope noble Lords will understand that I will write further. I say to the noble Baroness, Lady Finlay, that we have already sent the letter again, but if she requires one delivered by hand, I would be glad to do that. To state the obvious, the SPR is a simple idea, but it is technically complex to deliver. The greatest thing I have learned about this is that it is not all going to suddenly happen. Sometimes we are tempted to believe that it will, because we would like that, but it is not. It will develop and evolve, and that is why some of the questions asked do not have immediate answers. This is not a “trust me” situation; it is just the reality of developing a system and making it work. I emphasise that the SPR will build on existing approaches. For example, shared care records already exist, but they are built on local arrangements. In answer to the noble Lord, Lord Kamall, the Bill will give us a legal basis for an effective, nationally rooted SPR and make sure that doctors have confidence—which is the key thing—that they can share data with it. A balance will be maintained between a clear legal basis for the system and an agile approach to developing technology, as well as the secure and effective working arrangements around it. hansard.speaker: Kate Dearden
hansard.text: My hon. Friend rightly raises why this legislation will be important for consumers up and down the country who want to cancel their subscriptions. In our guidance, we are making businesses' responsibility clear to them and how they can ensure that information is very clear up front, as I mentioned at the start. It should be as easy to exit a subscription as it is to join; for example, if someone joins online, they should be able to exit online. That is a key part of the legislation and we will make that clear in the guidance, so that businesses can comply. For every unwanted subscription cancelled, consumers will save an average of £19 per month, which provides valuable breathing space and could mean a real difference to whether people are able to pay their bills. Subject to parliamentary approval, the draft regulations will commence on 1 January to ensure that we can protect consumers soon. I hope to have the support of all colleagues in Committee, and I commend the regulations to them.

hansard.speaker: Bradley Thomas
hansard.text: I wholeheartedly agree with my right hon. Friend; we must be very careful of unintended consequences. I implore the Government to review the implementation of the regulations on an ongoing basis to ensure that they do not put an unfair and unnecessary burden on businesses. The Opposition will not oppose this draft legislation. We know that unwanted subscriptions can cause significant financial trouble for households, and we want consumers to be protected from deceptive subscription providers. However, a careful balancing act is required to ensure that consumers get the protection that they need while ensuring that legitimate providers do not become unintentional collateral damage. I would be interested to hear from the Minister how the Government will ensure that that is achieved.

hansard.speaker: Matt Rodda (Reading Central) (Lab)
hansard.text: I welcome the hon. Member for Blackburn (Mr Hussain) to the House. As he mentioned, he has illustrious predecessors: Barbara Castle, Jack Straw and, more recently, Kate Hollern. I noted that he advocated very strongly for his community, and for more growth in his town, and I appreciate that. It is a privilege to speak tonight on the Finance Bill. I want to focus on four areas: the effects of the Bill on residents; its effects on high streets; entrepreneurs; and issues related to planning, and setting the right framework to encourage growth. The Budget offered breathing space and hope for the future in what we cannot doubt is a challenging international climate. First, residents in Reading are hard pressed by the cost of living crisis. Many of my residents live in older homes on terraced streets across the town, or in 1930s semis, and the cost of heating those homes is considerable, so I wholeheartedly welcome the Government's measures on energy—particularly the £100 of support—and the measures to tackle standing charges. I also welcome the measures to deal with the cost of travel, which are so important in getting people to work. The recent freeze in fuel duty, the freeze in rail fares and the reduction in bus fares will all provide residents with very real help in getting to work, and will help employers with the recruitment and retention of staff. I should also mention the very positive support for EV charging, which is important at this time. I would like to respond briefly to points made by the Lib Dem spokesperson, the hon. Member for St Albans (Daisy Cooper). I think she was somewhat over-optimistic about the idea of putting together two complex Government datasets to deliver help in a more targeted way. It is essential to have a simple system for delivering help.

hansard.speaker: Baroness Merron (Lab)
hansard.text: My Lords, as the noble Lord, Lord Kamall, observed, this has been a wide-ranging debate. There was some inevitability about that, because this is to do with patient safety, which we take extremely seriously. As noble Lords have said, patient safety is absolutely paramount. As I said, I am deeply conscious that every avoidable harm and death is one we should seek to avoid in the future. While we cannot turn the clock back for those affected—to whom I express my sincere condolences, as I know we all do—whether that be harm or death, our duty is to prevent that happening in the future. Every patient should have access to safe and high-quality care, but, as I have said, we know this is not always the case. I will say at the outset that I may not be able to cover all the points noble Lords have raised, but I certainly will try to address each of the issues raised in the amendments. I turn first to Amendment 106 in the name of the noble Baroness, Lady Pidgeon, which concerns action at trust level. I hope I can provide the noble Baroness with some reassurance that trusts are already accountable for reporting medical malpractice, including systemic cases. Therefore, while we understand the intent of Amendment 106, we feel it is not required simply because it duplicates the existing processes, local and national, for addressing the systemic issues—which have rightly been raised. CQC regulations already require trusts to have effective systems to identify, monitor and, importantly, address systemic risks to quality and safety. The NHS provider licence, which we spoke of in the previous group, also requires effective governance and safety reporting. Where governance does fail, NHS England has powers to intervene, and the Bill transfers those powers to the Secretary of State. I tur

hansard.text: The UK is not joining the EU digital identity wallet. This agreement does not commit us to doing so, or to adopting the EU's digital identity system. It does propose a digital partnership, but that is to deepen co-operation across our digital and technology sectors. That is the reason why it was warmly welcomed by the European chief executive of Vodafone on Friday.
